Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: For a witnessed-other trauma, strong flashback-like re-experiencing can occur, but this specific item implies reliving as if the traumatic experience were happening to the patient directly. With the rest of the profile emphasizing fragmented narrative memory and indirect threat cues, this item is somewhat mismatched to the witnessed-trauma context and is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile with a witnessed-other trauma unless there was clear perceived responsibility or preventability. No other items suggest responsibility, guilt about failing to intervene, or action-related causation, so this appraisal is insufficiently supported by the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Mali was 61, a sculptor who had spent most of her adult life working in a bright, cluttered studio at the back of her home, where clay dust collected on her apron and the smell of solvents and plaster usually felt familiar and safe. She had come in because, for months now, the ordinary sounds and scents of daily life had begun to unsettle her in ways she could not easily shake. The problem had started after an evening two winters ago when she was walking home from a neighborhood arts reception and witnessed a violent assault in the alley beside the gallery. A stranger had come up fast from behind another man, and the sound that stayed with Mali was not only the shouting but the quick, heavy footsteps on the pavement just before it happened. In the confusion, a strong cologne drifted toward her from someone passing close by, mixing with the cold air and the metallic smell of the alley, and those sensations lodged together so tightly that even now a whiff of perfume could bring the whole scene back with startling force.

At first, Mali tried to tell herself she had only been shaken by what she had seen, but she noticed that certain things now made her body react before she had time to think. Footsteps behind her in a hallway, a burst of cologne in an elevator, or the sense that something might happen without warning could leave her jumpy and physically tense, with her heart racing and her muscles bracing as if she needed to turn and protect herself. What frightened her most was how quickly night had come to feel unsafe. During the day she could still manage the studio and errands, but after dark she found herself checking the locks, listening for movement outside, and feeling that the house was not entirely hers to relax in. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the world was dangerous, and, more painfully, that there was something wrong with her for not being able to put the event behind her.

The memory itself was part of what kept the fear alive. Mali described the scene as more real and vivid than ordinary things, as if it remained fixed in a sharper color than the rest of her life. When she tried to tell her husband or the intake clinician what exactly happened, she often lost the thread and could not finish, her thoughts scattering at the moment she reached the alley. She could not make it into a clear story even to herself; it remained a fragment of footsteps, perfume, panic, and the sense of danger arriving too quickly. That brokenness in memory made her distrust her own mind, and the mistrust spread outward: if she could not hold the story together, she reasoned, then perhaps she was weak or defective in some fundamental way. The more vividly the memory returned, the more it seemed to confirm that the world was unstable and that she had somehow failed to cope like other people.

Those vivid recollections also taught her body what to fear. The smell of a stranger's perfume in a store, a set of footsteps coming up behind her in the studio corridor, or an unpredictable interruption at work could pull the alley back into the present, and in those moments she would feel the same sharp physical reaction she had on the night of the assault. In turn, the startle and vigilance made the memory easier to catch: once she was scanning for danger, any passing sound or scent seemed to cue the scene again, and the image returned with an almost bodily certainty. Mali began to move more cautiously through her days, turning her head when someone entered the studio, staying tense when she worked alone late, and avoiding the narrow alley near the gallery whenever she could. Even in the place where she made sculpture, where she once liked the quiet rhythm of tools on stone, she now found herself monitoring for footsteps and bracing against surprise.

Over time, the feeling that she must stay alert everywhere deepened her belief that the world was not safe and that something in her was damaged for not being able to feel otherwise. She had started sleeping lighter, especially at night, waking to small sounds and listening for movement before settling back, and she finally came for help when her husband noticed how often she paused at the door before leaving the house and how much she had shrunk the radius of her life. Mali was not only afraid of another sudden scare; she was afraid that if this kept going, she would lose confidence in herself entirely and stop going into her studio at all. What she hoped for, beneath the fear, was a way to feel safe in her own body again without having to live as though every footstep or passing scent meant that danger was already at her back.
